name: Authority bias
statement: People comply with an instruction from someone they read as a legitimate authority at rates far above what observers predict.
meaning: The claim is about the source of an instruction rather than its content. Three separate things travel under the name. The first is behavioural compliance with a command from a person occupying an authority role, which is what Milgram measured. The second is weighting an expert's opinion above the argument behind it, a judgement effect. The third is the argument from authority, a fallacy in logic. Only the first has the experimental literature described here, and treating the three as one idea is the commonest error made with it. What the experiments established is not a fixed human obedience rate. It is that the rate moves with the arrangement of the situation, and that people asked to predict it get it badly wrong.

origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: The 1963 paper reports a single condition. Milgram's pilot studies were completed in the winter of 1960, and the 23 conditions of the programme ran from August 1961 to May 1962. The famous paper is one slice of a series whose other 22 conditions were published later or not at all.

evidence:
Milgram's 1963 report covers one condition. Forty men aged 20 to 50 from the New Haven area, paid $4.50, were told to shock a learner for each wrong answer, one 15-volt step at a time, to a maximum of 450 volts. Twenty-six of the 40 went to the top of the board. Not one stopped before 300 volts, the point at which the learner gave up answering and pounded on the wall. Fourteen Yale seniors asked in advance to predict the outcome gave estimates between 0 and 3%, class mean 1.2%. Fourteen of the 40 subjects showed nervous laughter and three had uncontrollable seizures.

The 1965 paper reports the variations, and each condition described in it used 40 fresh subjects. Defiance rose as the learner was brought closer: 34% in Remote, 37.5% in Voice Feedback, 60% in Proximity, 70% in Touch-Proximity. Moving the experimenter out of the room and onto the telephone cut the number of fully obedient subjects from 26 to 9, chi-square 14.7 on 1 d.f., p < .001. Rerunning the study in a Bridgeport office with no visible tie to Yale gave 48% delivering the maximum shock against 65% in the corresponding Yale condition. When two confederate teachers broke off, 90% of subjects followed them. When the subject read the word pairs and a confederate pressed the switches, only three of 40 broke off. Forty psychiatrists at a leading medical school had predicted that a little over one-tenth of one per cent would reach the highest shock.

Haslam, Loughnan and Perry pooled 21 of the 23 conditions, 740 of the 780 participants, and report an overall rate of 43.6%, or 323 of 740. They dropped two conditions in which reaching 450 volts meant disobeying the experimenter. Their condition-by-condition table runs from 1 obedient subject of 40 in Carte blanche, where the teacher chose the shock level, to 37 of 40 in Non-trigger position, where a confederate pressed the switches. Eight of 14 coded properties predicted obedience in a logistic regression with a Nagelkerke R-squared of 0.30: the experimenter's directiveness, legitimacy and consistency, group pressure to disobey, the indirectness, proximity and intimacy of the teacher-learner relation, and the experimenter-teacher distance. The setting's prestige, the Bridgeport variable, was not associated with obedience at all.

Outside the laboratory, St Pierre and colleagues put 59 physicians and 18 nursing staff through a simulated rapid sequence induction in which a familiar attending physician created seven critical situations, including two potentially fatal drug orders. Participants identified a situation needing spoken intervention in 66% of cases, and 72% stayed silent. They challenged the attending in 28% of situations, and of those challenges 35% were oblique and 25% raised the problem without pursuing it.

examples.text: A man in a high-visibility jacket waves pedestrians off a pavement and they cross the road without asking who he is or what he is doing. The instruction is followed because of the role it seems to come from.

A junior nurse reads a prescription that seems too high and gives it because the consultant wrote it. The doubt was correct and was not enough, because the answer to it was the seniority of whoever had signed.

examples.tag: What a room says it would do
examples.text: Asked in advance, people say they would refuse an instruction like that, and say it with confidence. The distance between that prediction and what happens on the day is as much a part of the effect as the compliance.

replication.headline: The laboratory paradigm held up when Burger repeated it in 2006: 70% of his base condition went past the 150-volt point against 82.5% of Milgram's, chi-square 1.10, p = .29. The 1966 hospital field version was repeated in 1977 under the title 'a failure to replicate', but neither hospital paper could be read for this entry.
replication.detail:
Burger ran a partial replication of Milgram's Experiment 5, stopping the procedure at the 150-volt protest rather than continuing to 450. His justification was that 26 of the 33 Milgram participants who passed 150 volts, 79%, went all the way. Seventy people took part, 29 men and 41 women, aged 20 to 81, mean 42.9. In the base condition 28 of 40 continued past 150 volts, 70.0%, against 33 of 40 in Milgram's Experiment 5, 82.5%; chi-square(1, N = 80) = 1.10, p = .29. A modelled refusal condition, in which a confederate teacher pushed back from the table and quit, gave 19 of 30, 63.3%, and did not differ from the base condition, chi-square(1, N = 70) = 0.11, p = .74. Men and women did not differ. Burger names the ethical modifications. A two-step screen excluded about 30% of respondents at the phone stage and 47 of 123, 38.2%, at a clinical interview. Anyone who had taken more than two psychology classes was excluded. Participants were told at least three times, twice of them in writing, that the $50 was theirs to keep. The sample shock was 15 volts rather than Milgram's 45. The learner entered the room within seconds of the end, and a clinical psychologist ran the session with instructions to stop it.

The hospital line is the part of the story this entry cannot tell. Hofling and colleagues published an experimental study of nurse-physician relationships in 1966, and Rank and Jacobson published a paper in 1977 whose title calls itself a failure to replicate. Neither full text could be obtained on 21 September 2026. Nothing about their designs, their samples or their results is described here, because the only documents obtained for them were catalogue records.

A third result complicates the laboratory line. Perry, Brannigan, Wanner and Stam recovered an unpublished 1962 analysis by Milgram's assistant Taketo Murata linking each subject's post-experimental statement of belief to the shock level they reached. In 18 of the 23 conditions, subjects who fully believed the shocks were real gave lower shocks than those who did not; two conditions were level and three ran the other way. Across 656 subjects the fully believing averaged 19.05 shocks against 21.73, and a regression put the belief effect at 2.664 fewer shocks. Cross-tabulating Milgram's own five-point belief scale against outcome for 658 cases gives 37.7% obedience among those with the strongest belief and 68.8% among those with the weakest, Pearson chi-square 21.364 on 4 d.f., p < .001. Only 47.9% of subjects expressed no doubt, against the three-quarters Milgram reported in 1974.

study.cite: Burger, J. M. (2009). Replicating Milgram: Would people still obey today? American Psychologist, 64(1), 1-11.

limits:
The two hospital studies at the centre of the popular replication story could not be read, and the barrier is not a simple paywall in either case. The identifier for Hofling and colleagues (1966) resolves to an Ovid record which states that no abstract was provided and which gates the text behind a subscription login, while the publisher's own page at journals.lww.com answers a fetch with a Cloudflare challenge and HTTP 403. The identifier for Rank and Jacobson (1977) resolves to JSTOR, which returns an automated client challenge rather than any paywall notice. PubMed holds a record for each paper and an abstract for neither. Crossref confirms both citations, including the August 1966 issue date that PubMed indexes as 1967. Searches on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref, PubMed, the PubMed E-utilities, the OpenAlex location index, JSTOR, Ovid, journals.lww.com and general web search, and turned up no open copy of either paper. Every figure attached to them in secondary retellings has been left out.

Milgram's own numbers carry a second problem that no paywall explains. Haslam, Loughnan and Perry note that only 18 of the 23 conditions appear in Milgram's 1974 monograph, that tape recordings show the experimenter often going beyond the standard four prods, and that their coding of objective features cannot capture what participants believed was happening. Their pooled analysis treats each condition as an arm of one study, which is a defensible choice and not the only one.

The horn-honking literature is about a different question. Doob and Gross blocked 82 drivers at six intersections in Palo Alto and Menlo Park with either a polished 1966 Chrysler or an old Ford or Rambler. Eight men were dropped from the analysis, leaving 38 subjects in the low-status condition and 36 in the high. 84% honked at least once in 12 seconds behind the cheap car against 50% behind the expensive one, chi-square 8.37 on 1 d.f., p < .01; 47% honked twice against 19%, chi-square 5.26, p < .05. A parallel questionnaire went to 57 students and 55 were analysed, and the men in it said they would honk sooner at the expensive car. The authors report that reversal as a caution about survey methods. This measures whether status inhibits aggression, not whether people follow orders, and it is included here because the study is routinely filed under authority bias. Jann and Coutts combined the Doob and Gross design with a later one so that the status of the blocking car could be separated from the status of the blocked driver. Their abstract, read on 21 September 2026 from the RePEc record, reports that punishment came less readily when the two cars signalled a similar status. The working paper itself could not be fetched: the copy at repec.sowi.unibe.ch fails certificate verification here, and the Bern repository copy sits behind a proof-of-work bot check.

No effect size is quoted in the structured fields. Milgram, Burger and the Meta-Milgram synthesis all report obedience as proportions rather than as a standardised effect, and converting them here would produce a number that appears in no source.
misreadings:
The 65% figure is one condition of at least 23, and it belongs to two conditions at once. It is 26 of 40 men in the 1963 paper, the condition in which the learner says nothing until he pounds on the wall at 300 volts. Milgram also prints 65% in 1965 as the Yale rate he contrasts with Bridgeport's 48%, and there the comparison condition is Voice Feedback, which the archival counts make 25 of 40, or 62.5%. Milgram's variations run from 1 obedient subject of 40 to 37 of 40. Quoting 65% as the obedience rate of human beings inverts the finding, which is that the rate is a property of the arrangement.

The prediction study is usually mangled. Milgram's 1963 paper asked 14 Yale seniors, who gave a class mean of 1.2%. The figure of roughly one-tenth of one per cent comes from 40 psychiatrists and appears in the 1965 paper, not the 1963 one.

Obedience to an experimenter, deference to an expert and the argument from authority are three claims with one name. The Milgram literature speaks to the first. Nothing in it establishes that people over-weight expert opinion in ordinary judgement, and nothing in it is a result in logic. The fallacy has its own record at argument from authority, entry 417.

The experiments are often read as showing that people obey because they are told to. Milgram's fourth prod, 'You have no other choice, you must go on', was the one that came closest to a direct order, and the procedure ended if a subject disobeyed after hearing it. Haslam and Reicher argue that participants tend to go along when the experimenter justifies the shocks by the scientific benefit of the study, and typically refuse when he issues that direct order. They conclude that such people should be seen as 'engaged followers not as blind conformists'. Perry and colleagues add that a fifth of Milgram's obedient subjects doubted the shocks were real, and that the subjects who most firmly believed they were hurting someone were the ones most likely to stop.
